hints: Think about a candidate value x: can you make k + 1 consecutive pieces where every piece has total sweetness at least x?
For a fixed x, scan from left to right and cut immediately when the running sweetness reaches x. This maximizes how many qualifying pieces can be formed.
Feasibility is monotone: if x is achievable, every smaller threshold is achievable too. This suggests binary search on the answer.
A safe upper bound is floor(sum(sweetness) / (k + 1)).
title: Divide Chocolate Problem

notes: Each piece must contain one or more consecutive chunks.
Exactly k cuts create exactly k + 1 pieces.
The objective is to maximize the minimum total sweetness among the resulting pieces.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [[sweetness values], k]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialised integer return value

sampleTestCases.explanation: Make five cuts to form six consecutive pieces. One optimal division is [1,2,3], [4,5], [6], [7], [8], [9], so the minimum sweetness is 6.
There must be nine non-empty pieces from nine chunks, so each chunk forms its own piece and the minimum sweetness is 1.
Split the bar into [1,2,2], [1,2,2], and [1,2,2]. Every piece has sweetness 5, so the minimum is 5.

content.problemStatement: You are given a chocolate bar made of consecutive chunks, where sweetness[i] is the sweetness of chunk i. You want to share the bar with k friends, so you make exactly k cuts and divide it into k + 1 non-empty pieces, each consisting of consecutive chunks. You eat the piece with the minimum total sweetness. Return the maximum possible total sweetness of the piece you can eat by choosing the cuts optimally.

notes: Use 64-bit accumulation where needed for total sweetness; the maximum possible sum is 10^9 under the stated constraints.
The binary-search upper bound can be sum(sweetness) / (k + 1), because the minimum piece cannot exceed the average sweetness per piece.
For a fixed threshold, cutting as soon as the running sum reaches the threshold is safe because leaving extra sweetness in an earlier piece cannot increase the number of qualifying pieces.
solution.approach: Binary search the answer: test whether the chocolate can be split into at least k + 1 consecutive pieces whose total sweetness is at least a candidate threshold. A left-to-right greedy scan forms a piece as soon as the running sum reaches the threshold, which maximizes the number of qualifying pieces.

better.complexity: O(k * n^2) time and O(k * n) space.
better.description: Dynamic programming can process the bar prefix by prefix. For each number of pieces, try every possible previous cut and maximize the minimum piece sweetness over the partition.

optimal.complexity: O(n log S) time and O(1) auxiliary space, where S is the total sweetness.
optimal.description: Binary search the maximum feasible minimum sweetness. For threshold x, scan from left to right and start a new piece whenever the accumulated sweetness reaches x. If this produces at least k + 1 pieces, x is feasible; otherwise it is not. Feasibility is monotone, so binary search finds the largest feasible x.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n * C(n - 1, k)) time and O(k) auxiliary space for the cut-position recursion.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate every choice of k cut positions, compute the sweetness of all k + 1 pieces, and keep the largest minimum piece sweetness.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n log S), where n = sweetness.length and S = sum(sweetness).

followUps: How would you return one actual set of cut positions that achieves the maximum minimum sweetness?
